summary.text: For \(n=67\), the two distinct indices \(147\) and \(2055\) both yield the required residue sum: respectively \(1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67\) and \(1+3+9\cdot7=67\). Thus the multiplicity at \(67\) is at least two, providing the counterexample.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor\log_2 m\rfloor}(m\bmod 2^k)
\]
be A049802. Thus A383327 counts, for each positive integer \(n\), the indices \(m\) for which \(F(m)=n\). In the precise formulation under consideration, this count is written
\[
a(n)=\#\{m\in\mathbb N: m<2^{n+1}\text{ and }F(m)=n\}
\qquad(n>0),
\]
with \(a(0)=0\). The bound \(2^{n+1}\) is a sufficient search bound for the occurrences. For the disproof it is enough simply to exhibit two qualifying indices inside this bound.

We refute the claimed case \(n=67\). Consider first \(m=147\). Since
\[
2^7=128\le 147<256=2^8,
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 147\rfloor=7\). Its residues modulo the powers \(2^k\), for \(1\le k\le 7\), are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccc}
k&1&2&3&4&5&6&7\\ \hline
147\bmod 2^k&1&3&3&3&19&19&19.
\end{array}
\]
Indeed, \(147\) has residue \(1\) modulo \(2\), residue \(3\) modulo \(4,8,16\), and, because \(147=128+19\), residue \(19\) modulo \(32,64,128\). Therefore
\[
F(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67.
\]

Now consider the distinct index \(m=2055\). Since
\[
2^{11}=2048\le2055<4096=2^{12},
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 2055\rfloor=11\). Write \(2055=2048+7\). Its residue modulo \(2\) is \(1\), and its residue modulo \(4\) is \(3\). For every \(k\) from \(3\) through \(11\), the number \(2^k\) divides \(2048=2^{11}\), while \(0\le7<2^k\); hence
\[
2055\bmod 2^k=7 \qquad(3\le k\le11).
\]
There are nine values of \(k\) in that range, so
\[
F(2055)=1+3+9\cdot7=4+63=67.
\]

Both indices lie within the range used to define \(a(67)\): indeed,
\[
147<2055<2^{12}<2^{68}=2^{67+1}.
\]
Consequently the set
\[
T=\{m\in\mathbb N:m<2^{68}\text{ and }F(m)=67\}
\]
contains both \(147\) and \(2055\). They are distinct, so \(\{147,2055\}\subseteq T\), and therefore
\[
a(67)=\#T\ge \#\{147,2055\}=2.
\]
In particular, \(a(67)\ne1\). Equivalently, even if A383327 is viewed directly as the unrestricted number of occurrences of \(67\) in A049802, these two distinct occurrences already show that this number cannot be one.

Finally, \(67\) belongs to the conjecture’s specified set
\[
\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}.
\]
The conjecture asserts \(a(n)=1\) for every member of that set, and hence in particular asserts \(a(67)=1\). This contradicts \(a(67)\ge2\). Thus the conjecture is false.
